Merriam chipmunks (Neotamias merriami) exhibit a moderate basal metabolic rate when measured under controlled laboratory conditions. Respirometry trials conducted at a stable ambient temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] revealed a resting oxygen consumption of 78.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 78.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with expectations for a sciurid of its body size and reflects the energetic demands of its active, diurnal lifestyle in the chaparral and pine-oak woodlands of southern California. This relatively modest metabolic expenditure is consistent with the species' habit of caching food and entering periods of torpor during winter, strategies that reduce overall daily energy requirements. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive adults during their inactive phase to ensure a true basal state, and it provides a useful baseline for comparing the energetic costs of reproduction and thermoregulation in this species. Comparatively, the value is slightly lower than that predicted by allometric equations for a rodent of its mass, which may indicate an adaptive energetic economy in a habitat where food availability can be seasonally variable.

Reproductive output in Merriam chipmunks is constrained by a single annual breeding event, with females typically producing just one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year]. Within that single litter, the number of pups ranges from three to eight [N_R_i = from three to eight], a relatively moderate litter size for a small-bodied sciurid. This annual reproductive strategy, with a maximum of a single litter per year, is characteristic of many chipmunk species inhabiting temperate or Mediterranean-climate regions where a pronounced summer dry season and winter cold limit the window for successfully rearing young. The combination of a modest litter size and a low annual frequency means that annual recruitment is highly dependent on the survival of that single cohort. Field studies in the San Bernardino Mountains have shown that litter size can vary with maternal condition and local resource abundance, with females in years of high acorn and pine seed availability tending toward the upper end of that range. Under the thermoneutral conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], females are physiologically capable of supporting this reproductive effort without the added energetic burden of cold-induced thermogenesis.

The developmental timeline of Neotamias merriami begins with a relatively brief gestation period of 32 days [tg = 32 days] when the mother is maintained at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a duration that is typical for small sciurids and reflects the rapid intrauterine development necessary for the altricial young. At parturition, the wet weight of a newborn pup is approximately 4.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.3 grams], a value that was estimated through an allometric relationship derived from the congener Neotamias panamintinus. This tiny neonatal mass—representing only about five percent of adult female body mass—is characteristic of altricial rodents that undergo a significant growth spurt during the first few weeks of life. The pups are born hairless and with closed eyes, entirely dependent on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition. The gestation time is relatively short compared to the overall lifespan, allowing females to time parturition to coincide with the spring flush of new plant growth and insect availability. This tight synchronization between gestation length and seasonal resource pulses is a critical factor in the reproductive success of the species.

Weaning in Merriam chipmunks occurs approximately 21 days after birth [tx = approximately 21 days after birth] when maintained at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], marking the transition from complete milk dependence to the onset of independent foraging. At this stage, the young have opened their eyes and are beginning to explore the area around the natal burrow, although they may continue to nurse intermittently for a few additional days. The relatively early weaning age facilitates a rapid juvenile growth phase, allowing the young to accumulate sufficient fat reserves before their first winter. The age at which weaning begins is consistent with that of other small chipmunks and is likely shaped by the energetic demands placed on the lactating female. Post-weaning, the juvenile chipmunks must quickly learn to identify food sources, avoid predators, and establish their own burrow systems. This period of nutritional independence is a critical bottleneck in the life cycle, and juvenile survival during the first summer is often low. The weaning event also frees the female from the high energetic costs of lactation, enabling her to rebuild body condition before the onset of winter torpor.

Sexual maturity is attained relatively late in the life of Neotamias merriami, with puberty occurring 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] under thermoneutral conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This means that most individuals do not breed until their second spring, approximately one year after their own birth. The delayed maturation is thought to be related to the time required to reach the critical body mass necessary for successful reproduction; females must achieve a sufficient ultimate wet weight for females of 77.8 grams [Wwi = 77.8 grams] and males an ultimate wet weight for males of 71.8 grams [Wwi = 71.8 grams] to be competitive and reproductively viable. Males, which are slightly smaller on average, must still invest considerable time in growth before they can successfully compete for access to females. The maximum longevity recorded for this species is approximately five years [am = approximately five years] when maintained at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a typical lifespan for a small mammal that experiences high predation pressure in the wild. Thus, the species exhibits a relatively slow life history for its size, with a single year of growth before reproduction, a single annual litter, and a modest total reproductive lifespan of only a few breeding seasons.
